title: The Neuroscience of Affirmations, and Why You Need to Start Doing Them
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston argues that affirmations, often dismissed as a self-help cliche, have a genuine and well-documented research base behind their effect on performance, health, and academic achievement. His central piece of evidence is Carnegie Mellon psychologist David Creswell's 2013 study, which found that a brief self-affirmation exercise at the start of a school term could boost the GPAs of underperforming, chronically stressed students to match those of their low-stress peers by semester's end. Houston explains the mechanism through the idea that affirmations work on the subconscious drivers of daily behavior, citing Falk and colleagues' MRI research showing that considering one's own values activates the brain's neural reward pathways, and Sherman and colleagues' finding that affirmations let people view stressful events with a more rational, less threatened perspective. He extends the research beyond academics to physical health and weight loss, and to reduced defensiveness toward threatening information, before closing with a concrete, low-effort protocol: pick three short affirmations tied to core values, write them down, place them somewhere visible, say them aloud, and test them for 30 days to see whether behavior actually changes.
points: The Creswell study's specific finding — that a brief self-affirmation exercise brought chronically stressed, underperforming students' GPAs up to match their low-stress peers — gives a concrete, measurable outcome rather than a vague wellness claim, grounding the whole piece in a real academic effect.

Citing Falk and colleagues' MRI evidence that considering personal values activates neural reward pathways gives the practice a physiological mechanism, distinguishing it from a purely motivational or placebo-style claim.

The explicit tips for constructing an affirmation (tied to core values, short, written down, visible daily, said aloud, tested for 30 days) turn an abstract research summary into an immediately actionable personal practice.
quotes: When you hear the word affirmation, you might be tempted to think of it as a silly practice where people shout positive self-talk into their bathroom mirror in the morning. But research now reveals there are very real positive effects on performance, problem-solving, your health, and even the GPA of college students.
